summary.text: Exact divisibility follows by writing the numerator’s \(q\)-valuation as \(\sum_{s\ge1}\lfloor m/q^s\rfloor^2\) and bounding each corresponding denominator contribution using \(\sum_i i\lfloor N/i\rfloor\le N^2\). For \(m=np+k\) with \(k<p\), the added indices contain no multiple of \(p\), so they add nothing to the numerator valuation, while Legendre’s factorial formula shows the denominator valuation is unchanged because every quotient by a positive power of \(p\) is the same as at \(np\); subtracting these valuations proves the claim.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 U(m)=\prod_{1\le j\le m}\prod_{1\le i\le m}\gcd(j,i)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 D(m)=\prod_{1\le i\le m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac mi\right\rfloor!\right)^i.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{U(m)}{D(m)}.
\]
For a prime \(q\), write \(\nu_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the positive integer \(x\). We first prove that the displayed quotient is an integer, and then prove separately that the \(p\)-adic valuations of its numerator and denominator are constant as \(m\) runs from \(np\) through \(np+p-1\).

### 1. The denominator divides the numerator

We show that, for every positive integer \(m\),
\[
 D(m)\mid U(m).
\]
It is enough to show \(\nu_q(D(m))\le \nu_q(U(m))\) for every prime \(q\).

First calculate the valuation of \(U(m)\). For positive integers \(j,i\),
\[
 \nu_q(\gcd(j,i))
 =\sum_{s\ge1}{\bf 1}_{q^s\mid \gcd(j,i)},
\]
because the right side counts precisely the integers \(s\) from \(1\) through \(\nu_q(\gcd(j,i))\). Therefore, interchanging finite sums,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_q(U(m))
 &=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{i=1}^m\nu_q(\gcd(j,i))\\
 &=\sum_{s\ge1}\#\{(j,i):1\le j,i\le m,
                         q^s\mid j,\ q^s\mid i\}\\
 &=\sum_{s\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^s}\right\rfloor^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
All these apparently infinite sums are actually finite, since their terms vanish once \(q^s>m\).

Next, Legendre's formula gives, for every nonnegative integer \(N\),
\[
 \nu_q(N!)=\sum_{s\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^s}\right\rfloor.
\]
Indeed, each multiple of \(q\) among \(1,\ldots,N\) contributes at least one factor \(q\), each multiple of \(q^2\) contributes one additional factor, and so forth. Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_q(D(m))
 &=\sum_{i=1}^m i\,\nu_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac mi\right\rfloor!\right)\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^m i\sum_{s\ge1}
      \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/i\rfloor}{q^s}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\sum_{s\ge1}\sum_{i=1}^m i
      \left\lfloor\frac{m}{i q^s}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here we used the elementary identity
\(
\lfloor\lfloor m/i\rfloor/q^s\rfloor
 =\lfloor m/(i q^s)\rfloor.
\)
If
\[
 N_s=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^s}\right\rfloor,
\]
then another application of the same identity, with the two divisors taken in the opposite order, yields
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{m}{i q^s}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N_s}{i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus the inner sum is
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^m i\left\lfloor\frac{N_s}{i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Its terms vanish for \(i>N_s\). For each \(1\le i\le N_s\),
\[
 i\left\lfloor\frac{N_s}{i}\right\rfloor\le N_s.
\]
There are \(N_s\) such indices, so
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^m i\left\lfloor\frac{N_s}{i}\right\rfloor
 \le N_s^2.
\]
Summing this inequality over \(s\ge1\) gives
\[
 \nu_q(D(m))
 \le\sum_{s\ge1}N_s^2
 =\sum_{s\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^s}\right\rfloor^2
 =\nu_q(U(m)).
\]
This holds for every prime \(q\). Since both products are positive integers, unique factorization now implies \(D(m)\mid U(m)\). Hence \(a(m)=U(m)/D(m)\) is indeed an integer, and for every prime \(q\),
\[
 \nu_q(a(m))=\nu_q(U(m))-\nu_q(D(m)). \tag{1}
\]

### 2. Constancy of the numerator valuation

Fix a positive integer \(n\), a prime \(p\), and an integer \(k\) with
\[
 0\le k<p.
\]
Set
\[
 M=np+k.
\]
There is no multiple of \(p\) strictly between \(np\) and \(M\). Indeed, the next multiple after \(np\) is \((n+1)p=np+p\), and
\[
 M=np+k<np+p.
\]

Compare the products \(U(np)\) and \(U(M)\). The latter contains all factors \(\gcd(j,i)\) with \(1\le j,i\le np\), which constitute exactly \(U(np)\), together with factors for which at least one of \(j,i\) lies in the new interval
\[
 np<j\le M\quad\text{or}\quad np<i\le M.
\]
If, for example, \(np<j\le M\), then \(p\nmid j\). Since \(\gcd(j,i)\mid j\), this implies
\[
 p\nmid\gcd(j,i),
\]
and hence \(\nu_p(\gcd(j,i))=0\). The same argument applies when the new index is \(i\), using \(\gcd(j,i)\mid i\). Thus every factor newly introduced on passing from \(U(np)\) to \(U(M)\) has zero \(p\)-adic valuation. Therefore
\[
 \nu_p(U(np+k))=\nu_p(U(np)). \tag{2}
\]

### 3. Constancy of the denominator valuation

For every positive integer \(m\), additivity of valuations over products and powers gives
\[
 \nu_p(D(m))
 =\sum_{i=1}^m i\,\nu_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac mi\right\rfloor!\right). \tag{3}
\]
We compare this expression for \(m=M=np+k\) and for \(m=np\).

First consider the indices newly appearing in (3), namely
\[
 np<i\le M.
\]
We claim that \(\lfloor M/i\rfloor\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). Since \(n\ge1\), we have \(p\le np\). Also \(k<p\), so
\[
 M=np+k<np+p\le 2np<2i.
\]
Thus \(M/i<2\), proving the claim. Both \(0!\) and \(1!\) equal \(1\), so
\[
 \nu_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac Mi\right\rfloor!\right)=0
 \qquad(np<i\le M). \tag{4}
\]
Hence the new indices contribute nothing to \(\nu_p(D(M))\).

It remains to compare the summands for \(1\le i\le np\). We prove the slightly stronger assertion that, for every positive \(i\),
\[
 \nu_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{i}\right\rfloor!\right)
 =
 \nu_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np}{i}\right\rfloor!\right). \tag{5}
\]
By Legendre's formula, the left side of (5) is
\[
 \sum_{r\ge1}
 \left\lfloor
   \frac{\lfloor(np+k)/i\rfloor}{p^r}
 \right\rfloor
 =
 \sum_{r\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{i p^r}\right\rfloor,
\]
and the right side is
\[
 \sum_{r\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{np}{i p^r}\right\rfloor.
\]
For each \(r\ge1\), put \(L=i p^{r-1}\), so that \(i p^r=pL\). Since \(0\le k<p\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
Dividing once more by \(L\), and using the associativity of integer division, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{i p^r}\right\rfloor
 &=\left\lfloor
     \frac{\lfloor(np+k)/p\rfloor}{L}
   \right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac nL\right\rfloor,\\
 \left\lfloor\frac{np}{i p^r}\right\rfloor
 &=\left\lfloor
     \frac{\lfloor np/p\rfloor}{L}
   \right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac nL\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the corresponding terms in the two Legendre sums agree for every \(r\ge1\), proving (5).

Using (4) to discard the new indices and (5) for every old index, formula (3) now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_p(D(np+k))
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{np+k}i\,\nu_p\!\left(
       \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{i}\right\rfloor!
     \right)\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{np}i\,\nu_p\!\left(
       \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{i}\right\rfloor!
     \right)\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{np}i\,\nu_p\!\left(
       \left\lfloor\frac{np}{i}\right\rfloor!
     \right)\\
 &=\nu_p(D(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 \nu_p(D(np+k))=\nu_p(D(np)). \tag{6}
\]

### 4. Conclusion

Apply (1) at \(m=np\) and \(m=np+k\). From (2) and (6),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_p(a(np+k))
 &=\nu_p(U(np+k))-\nu_p(D(np+k))\\
 &=\nu_p(U(np))-\nu_p(D(np))\\
 &=\nu_p(a(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\). In particular,
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
 =\cdots
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as claimed.
